title: Does loan scenario modeling improve manager performance?
question: Among managers who previously did not model alternative loan scenarios, does beginning sustained scenario modeling improve average return on equity and risk-adjusted profitability, relative to their own prior performance and comparable managers who have not yet adopted it? Report expected outcomes at pricing and realized outcomes after funding separately.
hypothesis: After sustained adoption, managers improve average ROE and risk-adjusted profitability relative to comparable non-adopting periods/managers. Evaluate expected pricing outcomes and realized post-funding outcomes separately; effects may be absent, negative or inconclusive.
plan:
PHASE: protocol design only. No empirical execution is accepted by this draft.

1. Treat average return on equity (ROE) and risk-adjusted profitability as co-primary measures. Define four separate outcome series: expected ROE at pricing; expected risk-adjusted profitability at pricing; realized ROE after funding; realized risk-adjusted profitability after funding. Do not combine expected and realized measures.

2. Inventory source availability and approved business definitions before selecting fields. Verify units, annualization, risk/capital model versions, allocated equity/capital, income and loss treatment, and missing-value rules. Propose primary aggregation weights and sensitivity analyses; do not silently choose an unweighted average or a ratio of aggregates.

3. Define the exposure: transition from verified prior non-use to sustained use of genuinely different loan scenarios. Propose an auditable adoption rule, prior non-use window, minimum sustained activity, wash-in period and treatment of sporadic or discontinued use. Distinguish the manager responsible for a loan from the person who edited its scenario.

4. Establish one comparable selected/final pricing observation per opportunity at a fixed decision stage. Do not count every scenario as an independent loan. Keep funded and unfunded opportunities identifiable; link the funded subset to realized outcomes. State which population each estimate describes.

5. Propose a manager-by-time analysis comparing adopters with their own pre-adoption history and comparable not-yet adopters. Assess whether adoption timing and pre-trends support a causal design. Address experience, prior performance, product/borrower/risk mix, loan amount/term, bank policy, calendar conditions, coaching and self-selection. Choose the estimator only after data and assumptions are checked.

6. Specify pre/post windows and a common realized-outcome horizon or loan-vintage treatment. Address incomplete follow-up, manager turnover, transfers, missing observations and changes in metric definitions. Do not compare mature pre-adoption loans with immature post-adoption loans without adjustment.

7. Predeclare economically meaningful changes, uncertainty reporting, sample-size/power checks and interpretation across the four outcome series. A positive finding is not the success criterion. Report insufficient evidence when the sources or identification assumptions do not support an answer.

8. List required data and evidence: stable manager/bank/opportunity/loan identities; scenario creation/selection history; responsible manager and editing actor; quote and funding dates; approved expected/realized metric values or inputs; risk/model versions; and relevant covariates. Mark every unverified source and field as a gap.

9. Propose inspectable graphs linked to future run IDs: adoption/activity history; pre-adoption trends; adjusted outcome changes; expected-versus-realized comparisons; and uncertainty intervals. Label units, populations, aggregation and observation windows.

10. Return the refined question, hypotheses, estimands, data dictionary requirements, proposed method, validity threats, concrete next decisions and proposed Sol/Terra/Luna assignments. This request is one text-only planning call; it does not authorize worker delegation, data access or analysis runs.
